Confidence Interval for Omega Squared (Effect Size for ANOVA)

Source: R/ci_omega_squared.R
ci_omega_squared.Rd

Computes the point estimate of omega squared (\(\omega^2\)) of each effect of an analysis of variance and an exact, noncentrality-based confidence interval for its population value, for the partial and the total estimand (see omega_squared). With estimand = "all", the default, the function reports both; the interval from an effect's F statistic is an interval for the partial value, and the total has one only where it equals the partial value, in a one-way design (see Details). "total" or "partial" reports one estimand. The function takes a fitted model (aov, lm, or an aovlist from aov() with an Error() term) or an F statistic with its degrees of freedom and N.

Usage

ci_omega_squared(
  object = NULL,
  estimand = c("all", "total", "partial"),
  F_value = NULL,
  df_effect = NULL,
  df_error = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL
)

Arguments

object

Optional. A fitted aov, lm, or aovlist object. When supplied, the function returns one row per effect, with the stratum named for an aovlist. Give either object or the F interface, not both.

estimand

Which estimand to report: "all" (the default, both, with NA where the inputs determine no estimate or no interval), "total", or "partial". An estimand asked for by name for which the inputs determine no interval is refused (see Details).

F_value

Observed F-value from the fixed-effects ANOVA, or a vector of the F statistics of several effects tested against the same error term.

df_effect

Numerator degrees of freedom for the effect (one value for each effect, or one for all).

df_error

Error (residual) degrees of freedom.

N

Total sample size, the number of observations (nobs(object) is used for a fitted model). For an F from a design with an Error() stratum, give the size of the effect's stratum as N, as omega_squared and ci_eta_squared use it for such a fit: the number of subjects for an effect tested between subjects, and for an effect tested within subjects the stratum's total degrees of freedom, which is df_effect + df_error when the effect is the only one tested in its stratum. N must be at least df_effect + df_error.

conf_level

Desired confidence coverage; default 0.95. Used only when alpha_lower and alpha_upper are both NULL.

alpha_lower, alpha_upper

Optional Type I error on the lower and upper side. If both are NULL, a symmetric interval at conf_level is used. If both are supplied, conf_level is recomputed as 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper. The table records the coverage, 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper, as its level and, when the two tail areas differ, the areas themselves, which the line beneath the printed table, results_sentence, and the alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns of tidy() state; with a tail area of 0 the interval is a one-sided confidence bound.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_ci_anova, printed through dmar_tbl) with one row per effect and the columns effect; for each estimand reported, its estimate and limits, omega_squared_total, omega_squared_total_ci_lower, omega_squared_total_ci_upper, omega_squared_partial, omega_squared_partial_ci_lower, and omega_squared_partial_ci_upper; stratum (for an aovlist fit); and F_value, df_effect, df_error, and N. With the F interface effect is "overall" (the names of F_value, when it has them, or effect_1, effect_2, and so on, for several). N is the number of observations; the estimate and limits of an effect of an aovlist fit are computed with the size of its stratum, as in ci_eta_squared. The table records the confidence level of its intervals in its conf_level attribute (conf_level, or 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper when the tail areas are supplied), which the console prints beneath it and results_sentence reports; the estimand attribute records the estimand asked for, and the estimand_notes attribute names each estimate or interval that is NA with the reason, which the console also prints. tidy() gives one row per effect and estimand, with the limits in ci_lower and ci_upper (see dmar_tidiers).

Details

Point estimates. The estimates are those of omega_squared: the partial value, which for a fixed effect with F on \(df_{\text{effect}}\) degrees of freedom and N observations is $$\hat{\omega}^2_{\text{partial}} = \frac{df_{\text{effect}} (F - 1)}{df_{\text{effect}} (F - 1) + N},$$ and the total value of a fitted model with one error stratum, $$\hat{\omega}^2_{\text{total}} = \frac{\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}} - df_{\text{effect}} \mathit{MS}_{\text{error}}}{\mathit{SS}_{\text{total}} + \mathit{MS}_{\text{error}}}$$ (Hays, 1994; Keppel, 1991; Olejnik & Algina, 2000, Table 10). In a one-way design the two are the same number. Values below zero are reported as zero. An F statistic does not determine the total value, which the F interface reports as NA, and a fit with an Error() term has no total \(\omega^2\) (see omega_squared).

Confidence interval. The CI is constructed by Steiger's (2004, Proposition 1) confidence interval transformation principle: a CI for the noncentrality parameter \(\lambda\) of the F distribution is obtained (via ci_nc_F) and then mapped through $$\omega^2_{\text{bound}} = \frac{\lambda_{\text{bound}}}{\lambda_{\text{bound}} + N},$$ with the size of its stratum in place of N for an effect of an aovlist fit. When the lower CI on \(\lambda\) is not identified (i.e., the observed F is below the one-sided critical value), the lower limit on \(\omega^2\) is set to 0, matching the convention used in ci_pvaf. The population \(\omega^2\) and \(\eta^2\) are the same quantity, so the interval is the one ci_eta_squared gives (and, in a one-way design, ci_pvaf); the functions differ only in their sample estimators (an implication of the confidence interval transformation principle of Steiger, 2004).

Which estimand the interval is for. For an effect tested between subjects, \(\lambda/(\lambda + N)\) is the population partial value, the effect's share of the variance due to the effect and the error (Steiger, 2004, Eqs. 13 and 16), so the interval is for the partial \(\omega^2\). In a one-way design that is also the total, and the interval of a fitted one-way model is reported for both estimands. For an effect of a design with other effects, the total depends on their noncentrality parameters too, which one F statistic does not inform, and no interval is formed for it: with estimand = "all" its estimate is reported with NA limits, and estimand = "total" is refused with an error of class dmar_estimand_undetermined. The Details of ci_eta_squared give the sources and the within-subjects case.

Sums of squares in factorial designs. When a fitted model is supplied, the function reads the F-values from anova(), which in base R uses Type I (sequential) sums of squares. For balanced designs, Types I, II, and III give identical F-values; for unbalanced designs they differ. If Type II or III F-values are required, compute them with e.g.\ car::Anova(object, type = 3) and pass the relevant F / df into the F interface. See the Details of eta_squared on the coding of factors that Type III tests depend on. factorial_anova applies sum-to-zero contrasts itself and reports partial \(\eta^2\) and partial \(\omega^2\) with their confidence intervals for between-subjects factorial designs.

References

Bargmann, R. E. (1970). Interpretation and use of a generalized discriminant function. In R. C. Bose, I. M. Chakravarti, P. C. Mahalanobis, C. R. Rao, & K. J. C. Smith (Eds.), Essays in probability and statistics (pp. 35–60). University of North Carolina Press.

Fleishman, A. I. (1980). Confidence intervals for correlation ratios. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 40(3), 659–670. doi:10.1177/001316448004000309

Hays, W. L. (1994). Statistics (5th ed.). Fort Worth, TX: Harcourt Brace College Publishers.

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K., & Preacher, K. J. (2012). On effect size. Psychological Methods, 17, 137–152. doi:10.1037/a0028086

Keppel, G. (1991). Design and analysis: A researcher's handbook (3rd ed.). Prentice Hall.

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on \(\omega^2\) and its interval, and Chapter 7 on factorial designs.)

Olejnik, S., & Algina, J. (2000). Measures of effect size for comparative studies: Applications, interpretations, and limitations. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 25(3), 241–286. doi:10.1006/ceps.2000.1040

Steiger, J. H. (2004). Beyond the F test: Effect size confidence intervals and tests of close fit in the analysis of variance and contrast analysis. Psychological Methods, 9(2), 164–182. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.9.2.164

Venables, W. (1975). Calculation of confidence intervals for noncentrality parameters. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 37(3), 406–412. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1975.tb01554.x

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# 1. The F interface. Bargmann's (1970) example, used in turn by
#    Venables (1975), Fleishman (1980), and Steiger (2004): a one-way
#    ANOVA with five groups of 11 and an observed F of 11.221 on 4 and
#    50 df, at 95% and at 90%. F determines the partial value, which in
#    a one-way design is the total.
ci_omega_squared(F_value = 11.221, df_effect = 4, df_error = 50, N = 55,
                 estimand = "partial")
#>  effect  omega_squared_partial omega_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  overall 0.426                 0.226                         
#>  omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N 
#>  0.587                          11.221  4         50       55
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
ci_omega_squared(F_value = 11.221, df_effect = 4, df_error = 50, N = 55,
                 estimand = "partial", conf_level = 0.90)
#>  effect  omega_squared_partial omega_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  overall 0.426                 0.261                         
#>  omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N 
#>  0.565                          11.221  4         50       55
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%

# 2. One-way ANOVA from a fitted model: mean IQ gain differs across
#    the six grades of the pygmalion data (N = 310).
fit_one <- aov(iq_gain ~ factor(grade), data = pygmalion)
ci_omega_squared(fit_one)
#>  effect        omega_squared_total omega_squared_total_ci_lower
#>  factor(grade) 0.104               0.048                       
#>  omega_squared_total_ci_upper omega_squared_partial
#>  0.176                        0.104                
#>  omega_squared_partial_ci_lower omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value
#>  0.048                          0.176                          8.159  
#>  df_effect df_error N  
#>  5         304      310
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 3. Two-factor ANOVA for the manipulated expectancy treatment and the
#    measured grade classification (pygmalion data, N = 310). The
#    treatment by grade interaction is weak here (F = 1.19), so the
#    additive model is used.
fit_additive <- aov(iq_8 ~ treatment + factor(grade), data = pygmalion)
ci_omega_squared(fit_additive)
#>  effect        omega_squared_total omega_squared_total_ci_lower
#>  treatment     0.017               <NA>                        
#>  factor(grade) 0.028               <NA>                        
#>  omega_squared_total_ci_upper omega_squared_partial
#>  <NA>                         0.017                
#>  <NA>                         0.028                
#>  omega_squared_partial_ci_lower omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value
#>  0.001                          0.062                          6.519  
#>  0.001                          0.082                          2.787  
#>  df_effect df_error N  
#>  1         303      310
#>  5         303      310
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> NA omega_squared_total limits: No confidence interval is formed for the total omega squared of an effect in a design with other effects or with an Error() term: the noncentral F interval from the effect's F is an interval for the partial value, and the total depends as well on the other effects of the design (see the Details of ?ci_omega_squared).
